content.content:
set_graphic :: Patches what graphic clips are drawn from: name (another module), width, height, length (the graphic's own timeline in ticks; null ends it with the clip) and props, merged key by key — a null prop removes its key, except a key the module's schema has that an action on the clip animates (set_action_end's graphic): that one is set to the schema's default, so the animation keeps its start. A patch naming props or name is checked against the schema of the module it names, else of the one module every clip is drawn by; clips drawn by two different modules are refused for props. A clip that is not a graphic is an error. These are the BASE props; to animate one, add_action and then set_action_end.

write_graphic :: Writes the JavaScript module graphics/<name>.js in the project's package — atomically, creating graphics/ if it is absent — compiles it, and answers the compile of THAT text: ok, the module's meta and schema, and diagnostics [{level, message, line, column, frame}]. A module that does not compile is an answer, not an error: ok is false and the diagnostics say where; fix the source and write it again. With ok true, diagnostics are the module's top-level warnings (e.g. asset() outside render). clips lists the clips drawn by it, which redraw with the new text at once. A file write is not undoable and does not mark the project edited, but the text it replaced is kept — the last 10 per module; kept lists their revisions, newest first — and restore_graphic brings one back. Read graphic_reference first for the API.

get_graphic :: Reads the project's graphics/ folder. With name: that module's source, revision (the SHA-256 of its bytes), path, whether it compiles (ok, meta, schema, diagnostics), the clips drawn by it and kept, the revisions of its kept earlier texts, newest first (restore_graphic takes one). Without: folder, the folder's absolute path — where it WILL be when folder_exists is false; the first write_graphic creates it — and every module with its revision, ok and clips, warnings: what the folder's scan skipped or could not watch, in its own sentences, and history: [{name, kept}] for every name with a kept text, deleted modules included. The folder may also be edited with your own file tools: modules (<name>.js), fonts in fonts/ (.ttf, .otf) and pictures in assets/; the app sees a change within a moment. API.md and API.d.ts there are the reference, written by the app, and history/ is the app's too: the kept texts, which restore_graphic reads.

graphic_reference :: Answers the whole graphics API — the module's shape, ctx, the schema's types, the standard library, fonts, the sandbox, limits and idioms — as Markdown, for an LLM to read once before writing a graphic. Needs no project open; a project, when given, must name an open one. Help ▸ Graphics Reference opens the same file.

render_graphic :: Renders a module in graphics/ WITHOUT a clip — to look at it before placing it. png (the default) answers a contact sheet: the frames on a grid, each frame number printed under its cell, the cells scaled down (never the gaps or labels) so the sheet fits max_width; plus one sentence per frame that failed (drawn as its error card) or warned, with the engine's location. svg answers one frame's SVG text, its diagnostics and the ctx it was drawn with. ctx is a clip's: the canvas fps, durationInFrames from meta (else 5 s), the size from width/height, else meta, else the canvas. svg takes no path, background or max_width, which are the png sheet's, and writes no file. A frame at or past durationInFrames is drawn, with progress 1, as a longer clip draws it. A png sheet draws at most 134217728 px of frames (frames × width × height); past that the call is refused before any frame is drawn. No inspector control mirrors it: a person looks at the preview well.

set_track :: Renames a track, flips its four switches — the track header's toggles, Track ▸ Hide Video / Mute Audio / Lock Track / Solo — or sets its matte, Track ▸ Matte. hidden drops its picture from the composition, muted its sound; locked keeps every ripple, insert and range edit off it; solo silences every OTHER track in its container (the timeline, or a nest's own tracks) that is not also soloed — mute wins on a track that is both, and pictures are untouched. matte makes the track a matte for the track directly behind it in its container: its clips are not drawn, and what they show cuts that track by alpha, inverted alpha, luma or inverted luma — where the matte track shows nothing, the track behind shows uncut; a back-most matte track, or one in front of another matte track, cuts nothing. Its clips still sound. "none" makes it an ordinary track again. volume is the track's fader, linear 0–4 (1 is unity, 4 is +12.04 dB, 0 silent), multiplying every clip's own volume on it; pan is −1 (left) … 1 (right), a constant-power balance after each clip's own pan, and a mono source is not panned. Both are refused outside their ranges and play through nests: a nested clip hears its own track's and every enclosing nest clip's track's. compressor and limiter are the track's dynamics, run post-fader on its sub-mix — after every clip, its volume and its pan, compressor then limiter, the ceiling in dB

export :: Starts writing the timeline to a file and answers AT ONCE with {export_id, path, status} — ⌘E, the export sheet's six controls (format, size, frame rate, quality, loudness, range) in the sheet's own vocabulary, all but the frame rate — this exports at the document's rate, or on gif and apng at the format's own rate (12.5 and 25 fps). The export is a job in the Export Queue, run one at a time behind any other export already there; status is queued or running. An av1, av1_webm or vp9_webm job also waits while the app's other AV1 and VP9 exports would hold more than a quarter of this Mac's memory with it, and a later job may run first meanwhile (export_status's waiting says so). Follow it with export_status, which never waits — call it again after a pause until status is done, failed or cancelled — and stop it with cancel_export. The export_id lasts until Frame Job quits. Every refusal comes back from this call, before anything is queued: a bad argument, a missing folder, and a graphic clip whose module does not compile; a failure while writing comes back from export_status, failed with its reason (a graphic that fails during the export stops it with no file left, naming the graphic and the frame). ---
title: "Edit a module"
description: "Change a graphic's code in any editor, see the result as soon as you save, read what went wrong, and find the versions Frame Job kept."
---

import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

A module is the JavaScript file that draws a graphic. It's an ordinary file in your project, so you can edit it in any editor, and Frame Job redraws as soon as you save.

<AtAGlance
  menu={['Help ▸ Graphics Reference', 'File ▸ Restore Graphic Version…']}
  where={['Clip tab ▸ Graphic ▸ Source ▸ Open in Editor', 'Clip tab ▸ Graphic ▸ Source ▸ Reveal in Finder']}
  tools={['get_graphic', 'write_graphic', 'restore_graphic', 'render_graphic', 'render_frame', 'graphic_reference']}
/>

## Edit in any editor

<Steps>

1. Select a graphic clip and open the **Graphic** sub-tab of the **Clip** tab.

2. Open the **Source** section and choose **Open in Editor**. The module opens in the app your Mac uses for `.js` files.

3. Change the code and save. The preview redraws within a moment.

</Steps>

To use a different editor, choose **Reveal in Finder** in the same section and open the file from there.

The file is `graphics/<name>.js` inside the project package. Your own scripts and tools can write to that folder too, and fonts in `graphics/fonts/` and pictures in `graphics/assets/` are watched the same way. See [Fonts and pictures in graphics](/graphics/fonts-and-pictures/). The folder appears the first time something is written to it.

A module's name is lowercase letters, digits and `-`, starting with a letter or a digit, and at most 63 characters. A `.js` file with any other name is skipped, and the **Source** section lists it under **In the graphics folder**.

To write a module from scratch, see [Write a graphic module](/graphics/write-a-module/) and [The module API](/graphics/module-api/).

:::caution
Every clip drawn by a module changes when you edit it. To change one clip's look, use [Duplicate as New Graphic…](/graphics/manage-graphics/#duplicate-as-new-graphic) first.
:::

## Live reload

Frame Job watches the graphics folder, so you never reimport anything. When a module, a font or a picture changes:

- The paused preview redraws.
- The inspector updates, including a property list the module's new code changed.
- A playing preview picks the change up on its next frame.

Changes are gathered over about 100 ms, so a burst of saves lands as one.

Whenever Frame Job sees a module's code replaced while the project is open, it keeps the code that was there. The last 10 versions of each module are kept.

| --- | --- |

---
title: "Rename, delete and restore graphics"
description: "Rename a module and every clip follows, delete one no clip uses, bring back kept code, and copy a module to change one clip's look."
---

import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
import Shot from '@components/Shot.astro';

Each graphic in a project is a module, a file of code that any number of clips can share. These commands look after those files: rename one, delete one, go back to earlier code, or split a clip off onto its own copy.

<AtAGlance
  menu={['File ▸ Rename Graphic…', 'File ▸ Delete Graphic…', 'File ▸ Restore Graphic Version…']}
  where="Clip tab ▸ Graphic ▸ Source ▸ Duplicate as New Graphic…"
  tools={['rename_graphic', 'delete_graphic', 'restore_graphic', 'write_graphic', 'set_graphic']}
/>

The three **File** items have no keyboard shortcut. Each opens a small sheet with a **Graphic:** pop-up.

## Rename Graphic

Renaming a module changes its file name, and every clip drawn by it follows the new name, on the timeline and inside nests.

<Steps>

1. Choose **File ▸ Rename Graphic…**. The sheet opens on the selected clip's module when one clip is selected, otherwise on the first module.

2. Pick the module from **Graphic:** if it's a different one. The **New name:** field starts with the chosen module's name, and changes when you pick another.

3. Type the new name and choose **Rename**.

</Steps>

<Shot
  name="15b-rename-graphic-sheet.sheet"
  alt="The Rename Graphic sheet. A paragraph explains that every clip follows the new name and how to rename back. Graphic: is a pop-up reading lower-third, and New name: is a field holding the same name. Bottom left, small grey text reads lowercase letters, digits and -. Bottom right are Cancel and a dimmed Rename."
/>

A name is lowercase letters, digits and `-`, starting with a letter or a digit, and at most 63 characters. **Rename** stays dimmed until the name isn't empty and differs from the current one.

The module's [kept versions](/graphics/edit-a-module/#kept-versions) move with it. If the new name belonged to a deleted module, the two sets of versions join under that name. Past 10, the oldest are dropped for good, and those are the deleted module's.

The item is dimmed in a project with no graphics and while a nest is open, because a rename reaches every clip in the project. Leave the nest with <kbd>⌘↑</kbd> first.

## Undo a rename

When a clip uses the module, a rename is one undo step, **Rename Graphic**. **Edit ▸ Undo** puts the clips back and moves the module's file back to its old name with them, and **Edit ▸ Redo** moves both forward again.

A module no clip uses makes no undo step. To go back, rename it again.

Frame Job remembers the last 32 renames in a project to do this. An undo further back than that can leave a clip naming a module that has no file, and the clip draws the [error card](/graphics/edit-a-module/#the-error-card).

## Delete Graphic

Deleting removes a module that no clip uses. Its code is kept, so you can bring it back.

<Steps>

1. Delete the clips drawn by the module, or switch them to another one. See [Switch clips to another module](#switch-clips-to-another-module).

2. Choose **File ▸ Delete Graphic…**. The sheet always opens on the first module in the list.

3. Pick the module from **Graphic:** and choose **Delete**.

</Steps>

<Shot
  name="15c-delete-graphic-sheet.sheet"
  alt="The Delete Graphic sheet. A paragraph explains that a graphic clips still use cannot be deleted, that its code is kept so Restore Graphic Version brings it back, and that deleting is not an Undo step. Graphic: is a pop-up reading lower-third. Bottom right are Cancel and a blue Delete."
/>

**Delete** is the only confirmation. There's no second question, and deleting isn't an undo step and doesn't mark the project as edited.

Clips count wherever they are, on the timeline or in a nest. Fonts and pictures are left alone. The item is dimmed in a project with no graphics.

## Switch clips to another module

The inspector can't point clips at a different module that already exists. **Duplicate as New Graphic…** only switches them to a new copy. To move clips to an existing module, delete the clips and [insert that module](/graphics/insert-a-graphic/) again, or ask an agent to do it.

## Restore Graphic Version

Restoring puts back the newest kept version of a module's code, and it works on deleted modules too.

<Steps>

1. Choose **File ▸ Restore Graphic Version…**. The sheet opens on the selected clip's module when one clip is selected and that module has a kept version, otherwise on the first in the list.

2. Pick the module from **Graphic:**. The pop-up lists every name with a kept version, and a deleted one reads like `lower-third (deleted)`. Under it, the sheet says how many are kept, such as "3 versions kept".

3. Choose **Restore**.

</Steps>

<Shot
  name="15d-restore-graphic-version-sheet.sheet"
  alt="The Restore Graphic Version sheet. A paragraph explains that it puts back the newest kept version, keeps the code it replaces, and is not an Undo step. Graphic: is a pop-up reading lower-third, with 1 version kept in small grey type under it. Bottom right are Cancel and a blue Restore."
/>

There's no list of versions to pick from. The sheet always restores the newest.

The code a restore replaces is kept in its turn, and it becomes the newest. So restoring again returns to where you were, and the sheet swaps between those two rather than stepping further back. An agent can ask for any kept version.

Restoring isn't an undo step and doesn't mark the project as edited. The item is dimmed when no version of any graphic is kept. For when a version is kept, see [Kept versions](/graphics/edit-a-module/#kept-versions).

## Duplicate as New Graphic

Clips that share a module all change when it does. This writes a copy of the module under a new name and switches the selected clips to it, so you can change one clip's look and leave the rest alone.

<Steps>

1. Select the clips to split off.

2. In the **Source** section of the **Graphic** sub-tab, choose **Duplicate as New Graphic…**.

3. Type a module name. The field suggests `<name>-copy`, or `<name>-copy-2` and so on when that's taken.

4. Choose **Duplicate**.

</Steps>

Writing the copy can't be undone, but switching the clips can, as one step, **Duplicate Graphic**. Undo puts the clips back on the original and leaves the copy in the folder. Use [Delete Graphic](#delete-graphic) to remove it.

The button is dimmed when the module file is missing. When the selected clips are drawn by different modules, **Source** doesn't offer it.

## When Frame Job won't do it

On success, a sheet closes without a message. When Frame Job can't do what you asked it beeps, shows the reason in the sheet in its own words, and the sheet stays open so you can change your choice or choose **Cancel**.

| Item | The sheet says | What it means |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rename | `graphic name "My Title" is not a module name…` | The name breaks the rule above. |
| Rename | `graphics/title.js already exists` | Another module has that name. |
| Rename | `The name "title" is already drawn by clip 4 on the timeline…` | Clips left behind by a deleted module still use that name. Delete those clips or switch them first. |
| Delete | `The graphic "title" is still drawn by clips 4 and 9 on the timeline and clip 12 in nest 7…` | The sheet names every clip that uses it. Delete them or switch them to another module first. |
| Restore | `…was changed outside Frame Job and no longer holds the revision in its name; it is not restored…` | The kept file doesn't match what Frame Job stored, so nothing is written. |

**Duplicate as New Graphic…** reports the same two naming problems in an alert. Its clips stay as they were.

## With an agent

`rename_graphic`, `delete_graphic` and `restore_graphic` do what the sheets do, and answer in the same words when they can't. `restore_graphic` can name any kept version, not only the newest.

An agent duplicates a graphic with `write_graphic` of the module's code under the new name, then `set_graphic`. `set_graphic` can also point clips at a module that already exists, which the inspector can't do. A rename from an agent also waits until the nest is closed.

See [Tools: graphic fonts, pictures and packages](/mcp/tools-graphic-files/) and [Tools: graphics](/mcp/tools-graphics/).

## Related

- [Edit a module](/graphics/edit-a-module/)
- [The Graphic sub-tab](/graphics/graphic-tab/)
- [Insert a graphic](/graphics/insert-a-graphic/)
- [Share a graphic](/graphics/share-a-graphic/)

---
title: "Show video inside a graphic"
description: "Use a graphic as a matte so your footage plays through the shape it draws, and animate that shape like any other graphic."
---

import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

A graphic can't read a video's pixels, but it can shape one. Make the graphic's track a matte and the video behind it shows only where the graphic draws, or, inverted, only where it doesn't.

<AtAGlance
  menu="Track ▸ Matte"
  tools={['set_track']}
/>

## Show video inside a graphic

<Steps>

1. Put the video on a track, and the graphic on the track directly above it. See [Insert a graphic](/graphics/insert-a-graphic/).

2. Line the graphic clip up with the stretch of video you want cut. Where the matte track has no clip, the video shows uncut.

3. Select the graphic clip.

4. Choose **Track ▸ Matte ▸ Alpha**.

</Steps>

The graphic itself is no longer drawn. What it shows now decides where the video can be seen. To go back, choose **Track ▸ Matte ▸ Off**.

## Choose a mode

| Mode | The video shows where the graphic is |
| --- | --- |
| **Alpha** | Opaque |
| **Inverted Alpha** | Transparent |
| **Luma** | Bright |
| **Inverted Luma** | Dark |

**Off** makes it an ordinary track again.

## Write a module for a matte

A matte module is written and called exactly like any other, and the cut follows each frame as it animates. Fill the window in white so it works in every mode.

This one opens a rounded window with a spring:

```js
export const meta = { name: "Window", durationInFrames: 90 };
export const schema = { radius: { type: "number", default: 24, min: 0, max: 200 } };

export function render(frame, props, ctx) {
  const t = spring({ frame, fps: ctx.fps, damping: 18 });
  const w = ctx.width * 0.6 * t;
  const h = ctx.height * 0.6 * t;
  return svg(ctx, `<rect x="${(ctx.width - w) / 2}" y="${(ctx.height - h) / 2}"
    width="${w}" height="${h}" rx="${props.radius}" fill="#ffffff"/>`);
}
```

Its **radius** property appears on the [Graphic sub-tab](/graphics/graphic-tab/) as usual, and you can [animate it](/graphics/animate-properties/). See [Write a graphic module](/graphics/write-a-module/).

## What the clip's settings still do

The graphic clip's position, scale, opacity, crop and actions still shape the window, so you can move or fade it with the same controls as any clip.

Its blend mode, drop shadow and reflection do nothing. They're kept, and they apply again if the track stops being a matte.

The video's own drop shadow follows the cut-out shape.

## Good to know

Only the track directly behind the matte is cut, so tracks further back and the canvas show through the hole. [Matte tracks](/canvas/matte-tracks/) has the whole story, including what happens with two matte tracks in a row and how a matte looks on the timeline.

## Related

- [Matte tracks](/canvas/matte-tracks/)
- [Mattes inside nests](/canvas/mattes-in-nests/)
- [What a graphic is](/graphics/what-is-a-graphic/)
- [Edit a module](/graphics/edit-a-module/)

---
title: "Graphics playback and memory"
description: "How Frame Job keeps heavy graphics playing smoothly: drawing ahead, kept frames, Background render, and the memory they're allowed to use."
---

import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

A graphic is drawn from code, frame by frame, and a heavy one can take longer to draw than a frame lasts. Frame Job works around that by drawing ahead of the playhead and keeping what it has drawn. Nearly all of this is automatic, and the one thing you can set is [Background render](#background-render).

<AtAGlance
  menu="Frame Job ▸ Settings… ▸ Playback"
  keys="⌘,"
/>

## Drawing ahead while playing

While a preview plays forward over a project with a graphic in it, on the timeline or in a nest, Frame Job draws upcoming frames on spare processor cores ahead of the playhead. It uses one fewer core than your Mac has active.

It starts again from the new spot on play, on a seek, and on an edit while playing. It runs to the end of the timeline, or to the end of the in and out range while playback is looping inside it.

It doesn't run while the preview is paused or playing in reverse. Background render covers paused.

## Kept frames

A window keeps the graphic frames it has drawn in memory while it's open, so a stretch you play again comes from memory rather than being drawn again.

A frame is matched by what it draws, so changing a module or a property only redraws the frames that come out different. Frames go when the window closes or newer frames replace them. The least recently used go first, and frames Background render drew ahead give way last.

## Background render

When you leave Frame Job alone, the window you last played or moved the playhead in draws its graphics ahead of the paused playhead, so the next play is smooth from the start.

| Setting | What it does | Default | Range |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Background render** | Turns background drawing on or off. | On | |
| **Start after … seconds** | How long Frame Job must be left alone first. | 5 | 1 to 60 |

Find them in **Frame Job ▸ Settings… ▸ Playback**. They save the moment you change them, with no **Save** button, and they apply to every project. The ⓘ on the **Playback** heading explains them.

Background render needs a paused window that draws a graphic. It draws from the playhead to the end of the timeline, or to the end of the in and out range while playback would loop inside it, and it ends early if the [memory budget](#the-memory-budget) runs out. After that it waits for your next activity and the same wait before it runs again.

It keeps the processor busy while it runs, and it carries on while Frame Job is hidden or covered. It doesn't stop your Mac going to sleep. It only draws graphic frames, and it changes nothing in your project or your export.

## Set how long it waits

**Start after … seconds** takes a whole number from 1 to 60, typed or with the stepper. The field and the stepper are live only while **Background render** is ticked. A typed number outside the range beeps and the stored value comes back.

## What stops Background render

Any activity in Frame Job stops the pass at once, and it starts again after the same wait.

| Stops it | Doesn't stop it |
| --- | --- |
| A key, including a modifier key on its own | Moving the pointer |
| A click, a drag, a scroll or a trackpad gesture | Working in another app |
| Any edit, in any window | An agent's read-only call, such as `get_project` |
| Play, pause or a seek, in any window | |
| An agent's call that edits a project or moves a playhead | |

It never runs while any window is playing.

## The memory budget

The frames drawn ahead and the frames kept share one budget for all of Frame Job. It's sized to your Mac, with no fixed cap in gigabytes.

| Memory on your Mac | Budget |
| --- | --- |
| Normal | A quarter of its physical memory, so 8 GB on a 32 GB Mac |
| Short | An eighth |
| Critically short | Nothing. No frames are held, and each graphic is drawn when it's needed. |

The frames an [export](/graphics/graphics-in-exports/#parallel-rendering) draws ahead count too. Frames being drawn ahead come first, and kept frames give up whatever room those need.

Each playing window or export also holds at most 1,024 frames ahead, however much memory is free.

## What Frame Job skips

### Repeat frames

When a frame's SVG is the same as one already drawn, such as during a hold or in a static graphic, Frame Job reuses that picture. Your module still runs for every frame. Only the drawing of its SVG into a picture is skipped.

While an [action](/graphics/animate-properties/) moves a property, every frame comes out different, so a graphic that had settled costs a full draw per frame for the length of the action.

### The picture cache

PNG and JPEG pictures a graphic draws are decoded once and cached, so graphics full of pictures draw faster. The result is identical to drawing the original.

The cache is a sixteenth of the graphics budget, so it shrinks when memory is short. The least recently used go first.

## Good to know

Each frame has 250 ms to draw in the preview. Past that the frame draws the [error card](/graphics/edit-a-module/#the-error-card). An export allows 2 s, so a frame that fails in the preview can still export. See [Graphics in exports](/graphics/graphics-in-exports/).

Background render is a setting for a person. No agent tool reads or writes it.

## Related

- [Graphics in exports](/graphics/graphics-in-exports/)
- [Edit a module](/graphics/edit-a-module/)
- [Settings](/reference/settings/)

---
title: "Graphics in exports"
description: "What an export draws for each graphic, what stops an export when one is broken, and where a graphic's warnings show up."
---

import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

An export draws each graphic the way the preview does, so the file matches what you saw. A broken graphic never reaches the file: the export stops and tells you which one and why.

<AtAGlance
  menu={['File ▸ Export…', 'Window ▸ Export Queue']}
  keys="⌘E"
  tools={['export', 'export_status']}
/>

## What an export draws

An export draws each graphic as its module stood when the export was queued, whatever you edit next. Editing a module while an export runs doesn't change that file, and a job waiting in the [Export Queue](/export/export-queue/) draws the code it was queued with.

So you can carry on working on a module while an export runs. To get your new code into a file, export again.

## Parallel rendering

An export draws its graphics ahead on worker threads, one fewer than your Mac's active cores, so a graphics-heavy export doesn't wait on one frame at a time. The file is the same as drawing them one at a time.

It isn't used for an animated GIF or APNG, for a single frame, or for an audio-only export. Frames drawn ahead share the [memory budget](/graphics/playback-and-memory/#the-memory-budget) with the preview's.

## When a graphic won't compile

An export that would draw a graphic whose module is missing or doesn't compile isn't started, and any file already at that path is left alone. The message names each graphic and its first error:

> The export was not started: the graphic "title" does not compile — Unexpected token (line 3, column 7); the graphic "logo" has no module in graphics/. Fix the module and export again.

The check covers every graphic clip in the export's range, and every graphic in each nest reached from those clips. That's the whole nest, not only the part the export plays, so a broken graphic elsewhere in a nest stops the export too.

An audio-only export isn't checked, because it draws no pictures.

A job in the Export Queue reports this in its row when its turn comes, and it keeps the code it was queued with. Fix the module and export again.

## When a graphic fails partway

Compiling is the only check made before an export starts. A graphic that throws at frame 900 is found at frame 900. A graphic that fails partway through stops the export at that frame, and no file is left behind:

> The export was stopped at frame 900 of the graphic "title": … No file was written.

The frame number is the graphic's own, counted from its first frame. A frame fails when your code throws, when it takes more than 2 s to draw, or when its picture can't be made.

To find a failure before a long export, play the graphic through in the preview and watch for the [error card](/graphics/edit-a-module/#the-error-card). A frame has only 250 ms there, so the preview is the stricter of the two. A frame that takes between 250 ms and 2 s shows the card in the preview and exports normally.

## Warnings in a finished export

Warnings a graphic gives while drawing don't stop the export. Frame Job reports each distinct one when the file is done, with the graphic's name and the first frame it happened on.

- The Exporting sheet's finish line adds a count, such as "1 graphic warning (hover for details)". Rest the pointer on the line to see each warning.
- An [Export Queue](/export/export-queue/) row adds the count too, and its tooltip lists them.

Each one reads like `"title" at frame 12: message`. A warning given on every frame counts once, and an export reports up to 64 distinct warnings.

## The frozen clock

The clock inside a graphic is frozen, so nothing depends on when it's drawn and an export matches the preview. `Date.now()` is always `946684800000`, and `new Date()` is always 2000-01-01T00:00:00Z.

A graphic can't show today's date on its own, so give it the date through a [property](/graphics/properties/). A date you write out in the code, such as `new Date("2026-03-01")`, works as usual. The rest of the sandbox is on [The module API](/graphics/module-api/).

## Good to know

**Save Frame** has no such stop. A graphic that fails draws its error card, and the card is what's saved. See [Save Frame](/export/save-frame/).

## With an agent

`export` answers straight away with a broken graphic's reason, before anything is queued. A failure while writing comes back from `export_status` as a failed job, naming the graphic and the frame, and a finished job lists the graphic warnings. See [Export: start, then poll](/mcp/export/).

## Related

- [The export sheet](/export/export-sheet/)
- [The Export Queue](/export/export-queue/)
- [Graphics playback and memory](/graphics/playback-and-memory/)
- [Edit a module](/graphics/edit-a-module/)

The public user documentation: Astro with Starlight, one page per feature or tight family of

## Where things are

```

sidebar.mjs             every page's place in the navigation, in order
src/content/docs/       the pages: <section>/<page>.mdx
src/data/features.json  THE FEATURE LIST: what /features/ renders and what the proof reads
src/components/         AtAGlance (a page's facts), Shot (a screen in both looks),
                        FeatureIndex (the filterable list)
src/assets/screens/     WebP captures, written only by scripts/import-screens.mjs
src/styles/             the brand: the mark's inks, the app's faces, square chrome
```

## The rule that matters

**Every claim is written from the code.** A label, a default, a range, a shortcut, a limit or a
refusal is checked against `app/Sources/`, `core/src/`, `graphic/` or `mcp-proxy/` before it is
written, and the code wins over `docs/guide/`, a spec or an ADR. Never write what a feature
probably does. If the code cannot settle it, leave it out.

Nothing dev-only, deferred or unbuilt is documented. That excludes the dev tools (`snapshot_ui`,
`perform_menu_item`, `cancel_sheet`, `select_inspector_tab`, `play_preview`, `graphic_memory`,
`loudness_meter`, `land_recording`, `analysis_job`, `transcript_view`, `playback_rebuilds`,
`assistant_send`, `assistant_answer`) and every `-RCDev` launch default.

## Who reads this

Someone editing a video, who has never read this repository. They want to know what a thing does,
how to do it, and what will stop them. They do not care how it is built.

So a page never mentions: spec or decision IDs (`AU-12`, `§11`), road maps, phases, issue numbers,
source file or type names, `rc_*` exports, format version numbers, proofs, tests, or the history
of a feature. Internal words get translated: "refused" becomes what the user sees ("Frame Job
won't do this while…"), "the core" and "the op" disappear. A tool name is the one exception: the
MCP pages and `tools=` in `AtAGlance` name agent tools, because those are the product's interface.

## Voice

- Plain, direct and second person. Say what it does, then how. Short sentences.
- Open with what the feature is for, in a sentence or two, before any steps.
- British spelling in prose, as `docs/guide/` does (colour, centre, grey, normalise), and the
  app's exact spelling for its own labels (the **Color** tab, **Normalize**).
- Contractions are fine. No marketing: never "powerful", "seamless", "effortless", "robust",
  "simply", "just", "easily", "unleash", "supercharge".
- Prefer a full stop or a comma to an em dash.
- State defaults, ranges and limits as numbers. Say what happens at the edges, because that is
  what a reader comes to a reference for.
- No filler sections. A page with nothing to say under a heading doesn't have that heading.

## Page shape

```mdx
---
title: Markers
description: One sentence, what this page helps you do. Search results show it.
---

import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
import Shot from '@components/Shot.astro';

What the feature is for, in a sentence or two.

<AtAGlance menu="Mark ▸ Add Marker" keys="M" tools="add_marker" />

<Shot name="04-editor.window" alt="What the picture shows, for someone who can't see it." />

## Add a marker

<Steps>

1. Move the playhead to the moment.
2. Press <kbd>M</kbd>.

</Steps>

## Options

| Control | What it does | Default |
| ------- | ------------ | ------- |

## Good to know

Limits, edge cases and what stops it, in plain words.

## Related

- [Snapping](/timeline/snapping/)
```

Every section is optional except the opening. Order the task sections as a reader needs them.

- **Headings** start at `##`, are sentence case, and name the job: "Add a marker", not "Adding".
  A feature in `src/data/features.json` with an `anchor` needs a heading that makes that anchor.
- **Menus** are bold with `▸`, spelled as the app spells them: **Clip ▸ Split**.
- **Keys** use the app's symbols in `<kbd>`: <kbd>⌘T</kbd>. Inside `AtAGlance`, pass the string.
- **Controls** are bold where they appear in a step: choose **Save**.
- **Links** are root-absolute with a trailing slash: `/timeline/markers/#add-a-marker`. The build
  fails on a link or anchor that does not exist.
- **Asides** are for what a reader must not miss, not for decoration: `:::note`, `:::tip`,
  `:::caution`, `:::danger`.
- **Screens** come from `src/assets/screens/`. A `name` is the file name without its look and
  extension. Use a screen only when it shows what the page is about, not when the thing is out
  of frame, and give it real alt text.

## MDX traps

MDX is JSX. In prose, `{`, `}` and `<` start code. Put anything like `{x}`, `<1 s` or `a<b` in a
code span, or write it out ("under 1 s"). `<kbd>` and every component must close. A line starting
with `import` or `export` is code. Leave a blank line after an opening component tag and before
its closing tag, or the Markdown inside won't render.

## Checking a page

```sh
node docs/site/scripts/check-pages.mjs <page.mdx>…        # parses, imports, links, captures
python3 tools/proof/docs_site_proof.py --pages <page.mdx>…  # internal words, local paths
pnpm build                                                # in docs/site: the last word
```

## Screens

The captures come from the screen catalog (`designs/screens/`, `tools/proof/screens.py`), so the
pictures are of the real app. To refresh them:

```sh
python3 tools/proof/screens.py --out <dir>                      # from the repository root
node docs/site/scripts/import-screens.mjs <dir> --used
```

**This site is public.** `import-screens.mjs` refuses a capture whose layout dump holds a local
path, and its `CROP` table is the only way past that, by cutting the region away. Settings needs
it: its MCP section prints the helper's full path. Never weaken the refusal.

## When the app changes

A user-visible change edits its page here as well as `docs/guide/`, and a new feature adds its row
to `src/data/features.json`. `tools/proof/docs_site_proof.py` runs in `make test` and fails on a
menu item or agent tool the site doesn't document, a feature whose page or anchor is missing, or a
page that names something internal.

---
title: "Edit a module"
description: "Change a graphic's code in any editor, see the result as soon as you save, read what went wrong, and find the versions Frame Job kept."
---

import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

A module is the JavaScript file that draws a graphic. It's an ordinary file in your project, so you can edit it in any editor, and Frame Job redraws as soon as you save.

<AtAGlance
  menu={['Help ▸ Graphics Reference', 'File ▸ Restore Graphic Version…']}
  where={['Clip tab ▸ Graphic ▸ Source ▸ Open in Editor', 'Clip tab ▸ Graphic ▸ Source ▸ Reveal in Finder']}
  tools={['get_graphic', 'write_graphic', 'restore_graphic', 'render_graphic', 'render_frame', 'graphic_reference']}
/>

## Edit in any editor

<Steps>

1. Select a graphic clip and open the **Graphic** sub-tab of the **Clip** tab.

2. Open the **Source** section and choose **Open in Editor**. The module opens in the app your Mac uses for `.js` files.

3. Change the code and save. The preview redraws within a moment.

</Steps>

To use a different editor, choose **Reveal in Finder** in the same section and open the file from there.

The file is `graphics/<name>.js` inside the project package. Your own scripts and tools can write to that folder too, and fonts in `graphics/fonts/` and pictures in `graphics/assets/` are watched the same way. See [Fonts and pictures in graphics](/graphics/fonts-and-pictures/). The folder appears the first time something is written to it.

A module's name is lowercase letters, digits and `-`, starting with a letter or a digit, and at most 63 characters. A `.js` file with any other name is skipped, and the **Source** section lists it under **In the graphics folder**.

To write a module from scratch, see [Write a graphic module](/graphics/write-a-module/) and [The module API](/graphics/module-api/).

:::caution
Every clip drawn by a module changes when you edit it. To change one clip's look, use [Duplicate as New Graphic…](/graphics/manage-graphics/#duplicate-as-new-graphic) first.
:::

## Live reload

Frame Job watches the graphics folder, so you never reimport anything. When a module, a font or a picture changes:

- The paused preview redraws.
- The inspector updates, including a property list the module's new code changed.
- A playing preview picks the change up on its next frame.

Changes are gathered over about 100 ms, so a burst of saves lands as one.

A save isn't an undo step and doesn't mark the project as edited. **Edit ▸ Undo** won't take your code back, but [kept versions](#kept-versions) will.

## Diagnostics

The **Source** section reports what the module says about the selected clip, grouped under headings. While the section is closed, its summary shows the number of errors or warnings, or the module's name when all is well.

| Heading | What's under it |
| --- | --- |
| **Compiling the module** | The compile error, or the warnings the module's top level gave. |
| **No errors or warnings at the clip's first frame** | Nothing. That frame drew cleanly. |
| **Checked at the clip's first frame** | What drawing that frame reported, such as a missing font or a picture that isn't in the project. |
| **In the graphics folder** | Files the folder scan skipped (a bad module or picture name, an empty file, a font that loads no face) or couldn't watch. Each has a **Reveal** button. |

Each row reads like "line 12, column 4 — message". Click the row, or its **Open** button, to open the module in your editor.

Every problem is one of two kinds:

- An **error** means nothing drew.
- A **warning** means the graphic drew anyway.

The line and column are the module's own, when they're known. Some things to know when reading them:

- For a timeout, they point at where the function begins, not the statement that ran long.
- A problem found while drawing also names the frame, such as "render returned undefined at frame 12 — did you forget `return`?".
- A warning from the module's top level, such as `asset("x")` outside `render`, has no frame. It comes with the compile, and the module still compiles.

The inspector only checks the clip's first frame. A problem that starts later shows up as the error card when the playhead reaches it.

When the module file is gone, **Open in Editor**, **Reveal in Finder** and **Duplicate as New Graphic…** are dimmed, **Revision** reads "missing", and the section shows `No module named "<name>" in graphics/`. When the selected clips are drawn by different modules, **Source** names them and asks you to select one module's clips.

## The error card

A graphic that fails draws an error card in its own box, in place of the graphic. The card is dark red with a 2 px bright red border and white monospaced text. You'll see it in the preview and in stills.

It appears for:

- a missing module
- a module that doesn't compile
- a throw from your code
- a frame that runs out of time, which is 250 ms in the preview
- a picture the drawing engine won't make

The card reads, line by line:

```text
lower-third · frame 42
over the 250 ms budget at frame 42 (InternalError: interrupted)
line 7, column 3
```

Its first line is the module's name and the frame, or `lower-third · does not compile`. The message follows, then the line and column when they're known. The frame number is the graphic's own, counted from its first frame.

An error card never reaches a movie. An export [stops instead](/graphics/graphics-in-exports/#when-a-graphic-fails-partway).

## Kept versions

Whenever Frame Job sees a module's code replaced while the project is open, it keeps the code that was there. The last 10 versions of each module are kept.

| Code is kept when | Code isn't kept when |
| --- | --- |
| You save from your editor | The file changes while the project is closed |
| An agent writes the module | Something other than Frame Job removes the file |
| You restore a version | |
| You delete the module | |

The code the module holds now is never in the list, and code kept twice is listed once.

To go back, choose **File ▸ Restore Graphic Version…**. See [Restore Graphic Version](/graphics/manage-graphics/#restore-graphic-version).

Kept versions live in `graphics/history/` and travel with every save. Leave that folder to Frame Job. Fonts and pictures aren't versioned.

## API.md and API.d.ts

Frame Job keeps two files in `graphics/` for an editor or an agent working in the folder: `API.md`, the reference, and `API.d.ts`, its TypeScript definitions.

They appear once the folder exists, and they never create it. Frame Job writes them again whenever they differ from its own copy, so any edit you make to them is lost.

**Help ▸ Graphics Reference** opens the same reference in your default Markdown app, with or without a project open.

## How many files are watched

Frame Job watches the graphics folder itself, its `fonts/` and `assets/` folders, and the first 16 files one by one: modules first, then fonts, then pictures, each in name order.

That only matters in a folder with more than 16 files. An editor that saves by swapping in a new file is always seen. A save that rewrites a later file in place may not show until something else in the folder changes.

## Good to know

- In an untitled project, graphics live in a temporary folder and move into the package when you first save. A file you already have open in an editor is left at the old path, so choose **Open in Editor** again after saving.
- Saves less than about 100 ms apart count as one, so only the code from before the burst is kept.

## With an agent

An agent reads a module with `get_graphic` and writes one with `write_graphic`, or edits the folder with its own file tools. `write_graphic` answers with the compile of the code it wrote, so an agent sees each problem's level, message, line, column and frame straight away, and a module that doesn't compile is an answer rather than a failure. `render_frame` and `render_graphic` show it the error card and report what went wrong.

See [Graphics with an agent](/graphics/agents-and-graphics/) and [Tools: graphics](/mcp/tools-graphics/).

## Related

- [The Graphic sub-tab](/graphics/graphic-tab/)
- [Rename, delete and restore graphics](/graphics/manage-graphics/)
- [Write a graphic module](/graphics/write-a-module/)
- [Graphics in exports](/graphics/graphics-in-exports/)

---
title: "Rename, delete and restore graphics"
description: "Rename a module and every clip follows, delete one no clip uses, bring back kept code, and copy a module to change one clip's look."
---

import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
import Shot from '@components/Shot.astro';

Each graphic in a project is a module, a file of code that any number of clips can share. These commands look after those files: rename one, delete one, go back to earlier code, or split a clip off onto its own copy.

<AtAGlance
  menu={['File ▸ Rename Graphic…', 'File ▸ Delete Graphic…', 'File ▸ Restore Graphic Version…']}
  where="Clip tab ▸ Graphic ▸ Source ▸ Duplicate as New Graphic…"
  tools={['rename_graphic', 'delete_graphic', 'restore_graphic', 'write_graphic', 'set_graphic']}
/>

The three **File** items have no keyboard shortcut. Each opens a small sheet with a **Graphic:** pop-up.

## Rename Graphic

Renaming a module changes its file name, and every clip drawn by it follows the new name, on the timeline and inside nests.

<Steps>

1. Choose **File ▸ Rename Graphic…**. The sheet opens on the selected clip's module when one clip is selected, otherwise on the first module.

2. Pick the module from **Graphic:** if it's a different one. The **New name:** field starts with the chosen module's name, and changes when you pick another.

3. Type the new name and choose **Rename**.

</Steps>

<Shot
  name="15b-rename-graphic-sheet.sheet"
  alt="The Rename Graphic sheet. A paragraph explains that every clip follows the new name and how to rename back. Graphic: is a pop-up reading lower-third, and New name: is a field holding the same name. Bottom left, small grey text reads lowercase letters, digits and -. Bottom right are Cancel and a dimmed Rename."
/>

A name is lowercase letters, digits and `-`, starting with a letter or a digit, and at most 63 characters. **Rename** stays dimmed until the name isn't empty and differs from the current one.

The module's [kept versions](/graphics/edit-a-module/#kept-versions) move with it. If the new name belonged to a deleted module, the two sets of versions join under that name. Past 10, the oldest are dropped for good, and those are the deleted module's.

The item is dimmed in a project with no graphics and while a nest is open, because a rename reaches every clip in the project. Leave the nest with <kbd>⌘↑</kbd> first.

## Undo a rename

When a clip uses the module, a rename is one undo step, **Rename Graphic**. **Edit ▸ Undo** puts the clips back and moves the module's file back to its old name with them, and **Edit ▸ Redo** moves both forward again.

A module no clip uses makes no undo step. To go back, rename it again.

Frame Job remembers the last 32 renames in a project to do this. An undo further back than that can leave a clip naming a module that has no file, and the clip draws the [error card](/graphics/edit-a-module/#the-error-card).

## Delete Graphic

Deleting removes a module that no clip uses. Its code is kept, so you can bring it back.

<Steps>

1. Delete the clips drawn by the module, or switch them to another one. See [Switch clips to another module](#switch-clips-to-another-module).

2. Choose **File ▸ Delete Graphic…**. The sheet always opens on the first module in the list.

3. Pick the module from **Graphic:** and choose **Delete**.

</Steps>

<Shot
  name="15c-delete-graphic-sheet.sheet"
  alt="The Delete Graphic sheet. A paragraph explains that a graphic clips still use cannot be deleted, that its code is kept so Restore Graphic Version brings it back, and that deleting is not an Undo step. Graphic: is a pop-up reading lower-third. Bottom right are Cancel and a blue Delete."
/>

**Delete** is the only confirmation. There's no second question, and deleting isn't an undo step and doesn't mark the project as edited.

Clips count wherever they are, on the timeline or in a nest. Fonts and pictures are left alone. The item is dimmed in a project with no graphics.

## Switch clips to another module

The inspector can't point clips at a different module that already exists. **Duplicate as New Graphic…** only switches them to a new copy. To move clips to an existing module, delete the clips and [insert that module](/graphics/insert-a-graphic/) again, or ask an agent to do it.

## Restore Graphic Version

Restoring puts back the newest kept version of a module's code, and it works on deleted modules too.

<Steps>

1. Choose **File ▸ Restore Graphic Version…**. The sheet opens on the selected clip's module when one clip is selected and that module has a kept version, otherwise on the first in the list.

2. Pick the module from **Graphic:**. The pop-up lists every name with a kept version, and a deleted one reads like `lower-third (deleted)`. Under it, the sheet says how many are kept, such as "3 versions kept".

3. Choose **Restore**.

</Steps>

<Shot
  name="15d-restore-graphic-version-sheet.sheet"
  alt="The Restore Graphic Version sheet. A paragraph explains that it puts back the newest kept version, keeps the code it replaces, and is not an Undo step. Graphic: is a pop-up reading lower-third, with 1 version kept in small grey type under it. Bottom right are Cancel and a blue Restore."
/>

There's no list of versions to pick from. The sheet always restores the newest.

The code a restore replaces is kept in its turn, and it becomes the newest. So restoring again returns to where you were, and the sheet swaps between those two rather than stepping further back. An agent can ask for any kept version.

Restoring isn't an undo step and doesn't mark the project as edited. The item is dimmed when no version of any graphic is kept. For when a version is kept, see [Kept versions](/graphics/edit-a-module/#kept-versions).

## Duplicate as New Graphic

Clips that share a module all change when it does. This writes a copy of the module under a new name and switches the selected clips to it, so you can change one clip's look and leave the rest alone.

<Steps>

1. Select the clips to split off.

2. In the **Source** section of the **Graphic** sub-tab, choose **Duplicate as New Graphic…**.

3. Type a module name. The field suggests `<name>-copy`, or `<name>-copy-2` and so on when that's taken.

4. Choose **Duplicate**.

</Steps>

Writing the copy can't be undone, but switching the clips can, as one step, **Duplicate Graphic**. Undo puts the clips back on the original and leaves the copy in the folder. Use [Delete Graphic](#delete-graphic) to remove it.

The button is dimmed when the module file is missing. When the selected clips are drawn by different modules, **Source** doesn't offer it.

## When Frame Job won't do it

On success, a sheet closes without a message. When Frame Job can't do what you asked it beeps, shows the reason in the sheet in its own words, and the sheet stays open so you can change your choice or choose **Cancel**.

| Item | The sheet says | What it means |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rename | `graphic name "My Title" is not a module name…` | The name breaks the rule above. |
| Rename | `graphics/title.js already exists` | Another module has that name. |
| Rename | `The name "title" is already drawn by clip 4 on the timeline…` | Clips left behind by a deleted module still use that name. Delete those clips or switch them first. |
| Delete | `The graphic "title" is still drawn by clips 4 and 9 on the timeline and clip 12 in nest 7…` | The sheet names every clip that uses it. Delete them or switch them to another module first. |
| Restore | `…was changed outside Frame Job and no longer holds the revision in its name; it is not restored…` | The kept file doesn't match what Frame Job stored, so nothing is written. |

**Duplicate as New Graphic…** reports the same two naming problems in an alert. Its clips stay as they were.

## With an agent

`rename_graphic`, `delete_graphic` and `restore_graphic` do what the sheets do, and answer in the same words when they can't. `restore_graphic` can name any kept version, not only the newest.

An agent duplicates a graphic with `write_graphic` of the module's code under the new name, then `set_graphic`. `set_graphic` can also point clips at a module that already exists, which the inspector can't do. A rename from an agent also waits until the nest is closed.

See [Tools: graphic fonts, pictures and packages](/mcp/tools-graphic-files/) and [Tools: graphics](/mcp/tools-graphics/).

## Related

- [Edit a module](/graphics/edit-a-module/)
- [The Graphic sub-tab](/graphics/graphic-tab/)
- [Insert a graphic](/graphics/insert-a-graphic/)
- [Share a graphic](/graphics/share-a-graphic/)

---
title: "Show video inside a graphic"
description: "Use a graphic as a matte so your footage plays through the shape it draws, and animate that shape like any other graphic."
---

import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

A graphic can't read a video's pixels, but it can shape one. Make the graphic's track a matte and the video behind it shows only where the graphic draws, or, inverted, only where it doesn't.

<AtAGlance
  menu="Track ▸ Matte"
  tools={['set_track']}
/>

## Show video inside a graphic

<Steps>

1. Put the video on a track, and the graphic on the track directly above it. See [Insert a graphic](/graphics/insert-a-graphic/).

2. Line the graphic clip up with the stretch of video you want cut. Where the matte track has no clip, the video shows uncut.

3. Select the graphic clip.

4. Choose **Track ▸ Matte ▸ Alpha**.

</Steps>

The graphic itself is no longer drawn. What it shows now decides where the video can be seen. To go back, choose **Track ▸ Matte ▸ Off**.

## Choose a mode

| Mode | The video shows where the graphic is |
| --- | --- |
| **Alpha** | Opaque |
| **Inverted Alpha** | Transparent |
| **Luma** | Bright |
| **Inverted Luma** | Dark |

**Off** makes it an ordinary track again.

## Write a module for a matte

A matte module is written and called exactly like any other, and the cut follows each frame as it animates. Fill the window in white so it works in every mode.

This one opens a rounded window with a spring:

```js
export const meta = { name: "Window", durationInFrames: 90 };
export const schema = { radius: { type: "number", default: 24, min: 0, max: 200 } };

export function render(frame, props, ctx) {
  const t = spring({ frame, fps: ctx.fps, damping: 18 });
  const w = ctx.width * 0.6 * t;
  const h = ctx.height * 0.6 * t;
  return svg(ctx, `<rect x="${(ctx.width - w) / 2}" y="${(ctx.height - h) / 2}"
    width="${w}" height="${h}" rx="${props.radius}" fill="#ffffff"/>`);
}
```

Its **radius** property appears on the [Graphic sub-tab](/graphics/graphic-tab/) as usual, and you can [animate it](/graphics/animate-properties/). See [Write a graphic module](/graphics/write-a-module/).

## What the clip's settings still do

The graphic clip's position, scale, opacity, crop and actions still shape the window, so you can move or fade it with the same controls as any clip.

Its blend mode, drop shadow and reflection do nothing. They're kept, and they apply again if the track stops being a matte.

The video's own drop shadow follows the cut-out shape.

## Good to know

Only the track directly behind the matte is cut, so tracks further back and the canvas show through the hole. [Matte tracks](/canvas/matte-tracks/) has the whole story, including what happens with two matte tracks in a row and how a matte looks on the timeline.

## Related

- [Matte tracks](/canvas/matte-tracks/)
- [Mattes inside nests](/canvas/mattes-in-nests/)
- [What a graphic is](/graphics/what-is-a-graphic/)
- [Edit a module](/graphics/edit-a-module/)

---
title: "Graphics playback and memory"
description: "How Frame Job keeps heavy graphics playing smoothly: drawing ahead, kept frames, Background render, and the memory they're allowed to use."
---

import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

A graphic is drawn from code, frame by frame, and a heavy one can take longer to draw than a frame lasts. Frame Job works around that by drawing ahead of the playhead and keeping what it has drawn. Nearly all of this is automatic, and the one thing you can set is [Background render](#background-render).

<AtAGlance
  menu="Frame Job ▸ Settings… ▸ Playback"
  keys="⌘,"
/>

## Drawing ahead while playing

While a preview plays forward over a project with a graphic in it, on the timeline or in a nest, Frame Job draws upcoming frames on spare processor cores ahead of the playhead. It uses one fewer core than your Mac has active.

It starts again from the new spot on play, on a seek, and on an edit while playing. It runs to the end of the timeline, or to the end of the in and out range while playback is looping inside it.

It doesn't run while the preview is paused or playing in reverse. Background render covers paused.

## Kept frames

A window keeps the graphic frames it has drawn in memory while it's open, so a stretch you play again comes from memory rather than being drawn again.

A frame is matched by what it draws, so changing a module or a property only redraws the frames that come out different. Frames go when the window closes or newer frames replace them. The least recently used go first, and frames Background render drew ahead give way last.

## Background render

When you leave Frame Job alone, the window you last played or moved the playhead in draws its graphics ahead of the paused playhead, so the next play is smooth from the start.

| Setting | What it does | Default | Range |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Background render** | Turns background drawing on or off. | On | |
| **Start after … seconds** | How long Frame Job must be left alone first. | 5 | 1 to 60 |

Find them in **Frame Job ▸ Settings… ▸ Playback**. They save the moment you change them, with no **Save** button, and they apply to every project. The ⓘ on the **Playback** heading explains them.

Background render needs a paused window that draws a graphic. It draws from the playhead to the end of the timeline, or to the end of the in and out range while playback would loop inside it, and it ends early if the [memory budget](#the-memory-budget) runs out. After that it waits for your next activity and the same wait before it runs again.

It keeps the processor busy while it runs, and it carries on while Frame Job is hidden or covered. It doesn't stop your Mac going to sleep. It only draws graphic frames, and it changes nothing in your project or your export.

## Set how long it waits

**Start after … seconds** takes a whole number from 1 to 60, typed or with the stepper. The field and the stepper are live only while **Background render** is ticked. A typed number outside the range beeps and the stored value comes back.

## What stops Background render

Any activity in Frame Job stops the pass at once, and it starts again after the same wait.

| Stops it | Doesn't stop it |
| --- | --- |
| A key, including a modifier key on its own | Moving the pointer |
| A click, a drag, a scroll or a trackpad gesture | Working in another app |
| Any edit, in any window | An agent's read-only call, such as `get_project` |
| Play, pause or a seek, in any window | |
| An agent's call that edits a project or moves a playhead | |

It never runs while any window is playing.

## The memory budget

The frames drawn ahead and the frames kept share one budget for all of Frame Job. It's sized to your Mac, with no fixed cap in gigabytes.

| Memory on your Mac | Budget |
| --- | --- |
| Normal | A quarter of its physical memory, so 8 GB on a 32 GB Mac |
| Short | An eighth |
| Critically short | Nothing. No frames are held, and each graphic is drawn when it's needed. |

The frames an [export](/graphics/graphics-in-exports/#parallel-rendering) draws ahead count too. Frames being drawn ahead come first, and kept frames give up whatever room those need.

Each playing window or export also holds at most 1,024 frames ahead, however much memory is free.

## What Frame Job skips

### Repeat frames

When a frame's SVG is the same as one already drawn, such as during a hold or in a static graphic, Frame Job reuses that picture. Your module still runs for every frame. Only the drawing of its SVG into a picture is skipped.

While an [action](/graphics/animate-properties/) moves a property, every frame comes out different, so a graphic that had settled costs a full draw per frame for the length of the action.

### The picture cache

PNG and JPEG pictures a graphic draws are decoded once and cached, so graphics full of pictures draw faster. The result is identical to drawing the original.

The cache is a sixteenth of the graphics budget, so it shrinks when memory is short. The least recently used go first.

## Good to know

Each frame has 250 ms to draw in the preview. Past that the frame draws the [error card](/graphics/edit-a-module/#the-error-card). An export allows 2 s, so a frame that fails in the preview can still export. See [Graphics in exports](/graphics/graphics-in-exports/).

Background render is a setting for a person. No agent tool reads or writes it.

## Related

- [Graphics in exports](/graphics/graphics-in-exports/)
- [Edit a module](/graphics/edit-a-module/)
- [Settings](/reference/settings/)

---
title: "Graphics in exports"
description: "What an export draws for each graphic, what stops an export when one is broken, and where a graphic's warnings show up."
---

import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

An export draws each graphic the way the preview does, so the file matches what you saw. A broken graphic never reaches the file: the export stops and tells you which one and why.

<AtAGlance
  menu={['File ▸ Export…', 'Window ▸ Export Queue']}
  keys="⌘E"
  tools={['export', 'export_status']}
/>

## What an export draws

An export draws each graphic as its module stood when the export was queued, whatever you edit next. Editing a module while an export runs doesn't change that file, and a job waiting in the [Export Queue](/export/export-queue/) draws the code it was queued with.

So you can carry on working on a module while an export runs. To get your new code into a file, export again.

## Parallel rendering

An export draws its graphics ahead on worker threads, one fewer than your Mac's active cores, so a graphics-heavy export doesn't wait on one frame at a time. The file is the same as drawing them one at a time.

It isn't used for an animated GIF or APNG, for a single frame, or for an audio-only export. Frames drawn ahead share the [memory budget](/graphics/playback-and-memory/#the-memory-budget) with the preview's.

## When a graphic won't compile

An export that would draw a graphic whose module is missing or doesn't compile isn't started, and any file already at that path is left alone. The message names each graphic and its first error:

> The export was not started: the graphic "title" does not compile — Unexpected token (line 3, column 7); the graphic "logo" has no module in graphics/. Fix the module and export again.

The check covers every graphic clip in the export's range, and every graphic in each nest reached from those clips. That's the whole nest, not only the part the export plays, so a broken graphic elsewhere in a nest stops the export too.

An audio-only export isn't checked, because it draws no pictures.

A job in the Export Queue reports this in its row when its turn comes, and it keeps the code it was queued with. Fix the module and export again.

## When a graphic fails partway

Compiling is the only check made before an export starts. A graphic that throws at frame 900 is found at frame 900. A graphic that fails partway through stops the export at that frame, and no file is left behind:

> The export was stopped at frame 900 of the graphic "title": … No file was written.

The frame number is the graphic's own, counted from its first frame. A frame fails when your code throws, when it takes more than 2 s to draw, or when its picture can't be made.

To find a failure before a long export, play the graphic through in the preview and watch for the [error card](/graphics/edit-a-module/#the-error-card). A frame has only 250 ms there, so the preview is the stricter of the two. A frame that takes between 250 ms and 2 s shows the card in the preview and exports normally.

## Warnings in a finished export

Warnings a graphic gives while drawing don't stop the export. Frame Job reports each distinct one when the file is done, with the graphic's name and the first frame it happened on.

- The Exporting sheet's finish line adds a count, such as "1 graphic warning (hover for details)". Rest the pointer on the line to see each warning.
- An [Export Queue](/export/export-queue/) row adds the count too, and its tooltip lists them.

Each one reads like `"title" at frame 12: message`. A warning given on every frame counts once, and an export reports up to 64 distinct warnings.

## The frozen clock

The clock inside a graphic is frozen, so nothing depends on when it's drawn and an export matches the preview. `Date.now()` is always `946684800000`, and `new Date()` is always 2000-01-01T00:00:00Z.

A graphic can't show today's date on its own, so give it the date through a [property](/graphics/properties/). A date you write out in the code, such as `new Date("2026-03-01")`, works as usual. The rest of the sandbox is on [The module API](/graphics/module-api/).

## Good to know

**Save Frame** has no such stop. A graphic that fails draws its error card, and the card is what's saved. See [Save Frame](/export/save-frame/).

## With an agent

`export` answers straight away with a broken graphic's reason, before anything is queued. A failure while writing comes back from `export_status` as a failed job, naming the graphic and the frame, and a finished job lists the graphic warnings. See [Export: start, then poll](/mcp/export/).

## Related

- [The export sheet](/export/export-sheet/)
- [The Export Queue](/export/export-queue/)
- [Graphics playback and memory](/graphics/playback-and-memory/)
- [Edit a module](/graphics/edit-a-module/)

Contents of /Users/kevingalligan/devel/framejob/.claude/worktrees/help-docs/docs/site/CLAUDE.md:

# CLAUDE.md — the documentation site

The public user documentation: Astro with Starlight, one page per feature or tight family of
features. `pnpm` manages it, Node is pinned by `.node-version`. `README.md` has the commands.

## Where things are

```
astro.config.mjs        Starlight's settings: title, logo, fonts, theme, plugins
sidebar.mjs             every page's place in the navigation, in order
src/content/docs/       the pages: <section>/<page>.mdx
src/data/features.json  THE FEATURE LIST: what /features/ renders and what the proof reads
src/components/         AtAGlance (a page's facts), Shot (a screen in both looks),
                        FeatureIndex (the filterable list)
src/assets/screens/     WebP captures, written only by scripts/import-screens.mjs
src/styles/             the brand: the mark's inks, the app's faces, square chrome
```

## The rule that matters

**Every claim is written from the code.** A label, a default, a range, a shortcut, a limit or a
refusal is checked against `app/Sources/`, `core/src/`, `graphic/` or `mcp-proxy/` before it is
written, and the code wins over `docs/guide/`, a spec or an ADR. Never write what a feature
probably does. If the code cannot settle it, leave it out.

Nothing dev-only, deferred or unbuilt is documented. That excludes the dev tools (`snapshot_ui`,
`perform_menu_item`, `cancel_sheet`, `select_inspector_tab`, `play_preview`, `graphic_memory`,
`loudness_meter`, `land_recording`, `analysis_job`, `transcript_view`, `playback_rebuilds`,
`assistant_send`, `assistant_answer`) and every `-RCDev` launch default.

## Who reads this

Someone editing a video, who has never read this repository. They want to know what a thing does,
how to do it, and what will stop them. They do not care how it is built.

So a page never mentions: spec or decision IDs (`AU-12`, `§11`), road maps, phases, issue numbers,
source file or type names, `rc_*` exports, format version numbers, proofs, tests, or the history
of a feature. Internal words get translated: "refused" becomes what the user sees ("Frame Job
won't do this while…"), "the core" and "the op" disappear. A tool name is the one exception: the
MCP pages and `tools=` in `AtAGlance` name agent tools, because those are the product's interface.

## Voice

- Plain, direct and second person. Say what it does, then how. Short sentences.
- Open with what the feature is for, in a sentence or two, before any steps.
- British spelling in prose, as `docs/guide/` does (colour, centre, grey, normalise), and the
  app's exact spelling for its own labels (the **Color** tab, **Normalize**).
- Contractions are fine. No marketing: never "powerful", "seamless", "effortless", "robust",
  "simply", "just", "easily", "unleash", "supercharge".
- Prefer a full stop or a comma to an em dash.
- State defaults, ranges and limits as numbers. Say what happens at the edges, because that is
  what a reader comes to a reference for.
- No filler sections. A page with nothing to say under a heading doesn't have that heading.

## Page shape

```mdx
---
title: Markers
description: One sentence, what this page helps you do. Search results show it.
---

import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
import Shot from '@components/Shot.astro';

What the feature is for, in a sentence or two.

<AtAGlance menu="Mark ▸ Add Marker" keys="M" tools="add_marker" />

<Shot name="04-editor.window" alt="What the picture shows, for someone who can't see it." />

## Add a marker

<Steps>

1. Move the playhead to the moment.
2. Press <kbd>M</kbd>.

</Steps>

## Options

| Control | What it does | Default |
| ------- | ------------ | ------- |

## Good to know

Limits, edge cases and what stops it, in plain words.

## Related

- [Snapping](/timeline/snapping/)
```

Every section is optional except the opening. Order the task sections as a reader needs them.

- **Headings** start at `##`, are sentence case, and name the job: "Add a marker", not "Adding".
  A feature in `src/data/features.json` with an `anchor` needs a heading that makes that anchor.
- **Menus** are bold with `▸`, spelled as the app spells them: **Clip ▸ Split**.
- **Keys** use the app's symbols in `<kbd>`: <kbd>⌘T</kbd>. Inside `AtAGlance`, pass the string.
- **Controls** are bold where they appear in a step: choose **Save**.
- **Links** are root-absolute with a trailing slash: `/timeline/markers/#add-a-marker`. The build
  fails on a link or anchor that does not exist.
- **Asides** are for what a reader must not miss, not for decoration: `:::note`, `:::tip`,
  `:::caution`, `:::danger`.
- **Screens** come from `src/assets/screens/`. A `name` is the file name without its look and
  extension. Use a screen only when it shows what the page is about, not when the thing is out
  of frame, and give it real alt text.

## MDX traps

MDX is JSX. In prose, `{`, `}` and `<` start code. Put anything like `{x}`, `<1 s` or `a<b` in a
code span, or write it out ("under 1 s"). `<kbd>` and every component must close. A line starting
with `import` or `export` is code. Leave a blank line after an opening component tag and before
its closing tag, or the Markdown inside won't render.

## Checking a page

```sh
node docs/site/scripts/check-pages.mjs <page.mdx>…        # parses, imports, links, captures
python3 tools/proof/docs_site_proof.py --pages <page.mdx>…  # internal words, local paths
pnpm build                                                # in docs/site: the last word
```

## Screens

The captures come from the screen catalog (`designs/screens/`, `tools/proof/screens.py`), so the
pictures are of the real app. To refresh them:

```sh
python3 tools/proof/screens.py --out <dir>                      # from the repository root
node docs/site/scripts/import-screens.mjs <dir> --used
```

**This site is public.** `import-screens.mjs` refuses a capture whose layout dump holds a local
path, and its `CROP` table is the only way past that, by cutting the region away. Settings needs
it: its MCP section prints the helper's full path. Never weaken the refusal.

## When the app changes

A user-visible change edits its page here as well as `docs/guide/`, and a new feature adds its row
to `src/data/features.json`. `tools/proof/docs_site_proof.py` runs in `make test` and fails on a
menu item or agent tool the site doesn't document, a feature whose page or anchor is missing, or a
page that names something internal.

</system-reminder>

# app/CLAUDE.md — Swift app rules

Applies to everything under `app/`. Build/verification commands and the FFI
lockstep are in the root `CLAUDE.md`; the full design is
`designs/spec/` (§3–4 the UI, §7.4–7.8 the platform side; its `README.md` is
the index). The
long form of each entry below — why each file is the shape it is, and the
traps its history turned up — is `designs/adr/app-file-history.md` (the
full history, every size toll and measurement, is archived; see its
"Original" line); this file is what governs a file now. Files
are listed by family; a file with a header comment of its own carries its
detail there.

## File map

**The core's edge.**
- `ReelCore.swift` — with its `ReelCore+<Area>.swift` files, the only files
  that call `rc_*` (spec §11 CJ-8 (l)); a new wrapper goes in the file of its
  area. `ReelCore.swift` holds `ReelProject`
  (handle + lazily decoded `ProjectSnapshot`; `json`, `snapshot` and
  `planJSON` are memoised PER HANDLE, so keep handles rather than minting
  them; so is `sourceMap(_:)`, `rc_project_source_map` decoded and checked
  once per handle and clip, SR-20), timecode, snapping (export presets/sizes/settings are
  `ExportValues.swift`'s, a pure move, HDR H-1), `ReelSpeed.limits` (the
  core's speed range and audio ceiling, typed as `SpeedLimits` in
  `CoreValues.swift` — no Swift file types a speed bound), `ReelColor` (`rc_normalise_color`, G-25) and `ReelAgentSocket` (below);
  `ReelCore+MediaFiles.swift` holds the media files the core reads or writes —
  `ReelContainer` (`rc_container_*`, a WebM/Matroska file's index, #216-R), `ReelCube`,
  `ReelHDR10` (`rc_hdr10_peak`, spec §11 HD-6; `av1Peak`, `rc_hdr10_av1_peak`, HD-18;
  `stillPeak`, `rc_hdr10_still_peak`, HD-20), `ReelAV1` and `ReelWebM` (`rc_webm_*`, the
  `av1_webm` writer, spec §11 CX-15) — `ReelCore+Cursor.swift` holds `ReelCursor`
  (`rc_cursor_open`, `rc_cursor_free`: a cursor file's open, which is its check, spec
  §11 CU-9, CU-15; road map creator-jobs CU1a; and `query`, `rc_cursor_query`'s one
  JSON request, CU2, spec §11 CU-25, and the static `query(_:tracks:project:)`, the
  same call over n tracks with a project (`plan_zooms`, CU-70)) — `ReelCore+Framing.swift`
  holds `SpeakerMatch` and `ReelProject.speakerMatch` (`rc_project_speaker_match`, road map
  creator-jobs VR6b, spec §11 VR-65: the face-to-microphone match Make Vertical's sheet
  confirms) — and `ReelCore+Graphics.swift` the graphics engine's
  wrappers (below), with `ReelGraphicPackage` (`rc_graphic_package_write`, G-46; `read`,
  `rc_graphic_package_read`, G-47), `GraphicLibrary.usage()` (`rc_graphic_library_usage`)
  and `GraphicLibrary.imageCache(limit:)` (`rc_graphic_image_cache`, G-39) — both pure moves
  out of `ReelCore.swift` (road map creator-jobs CJ0d, T15); `ReelCoreError`, `Fps.ffiPair` and `ReelTime`'s
  seconds conversions are `CoreValues.swift`'s (G6 phase 5's toll T2 and speed ramps SR4-0,
  pure moves); the typed patches are `TypedPatches.swift`'s (`VideoPatch`,
  `AudioPatch`, `ClipPatch`, the `ActionPatch` extension; a pure move, B73),
  `TextPatch` (with `case`, `words` and `word_style`) is `TextPatch.swift`'s,

**Frozen files.** `EditorViewController.swift`, `TimelineView.swift`,
`PreviewCanvasView.swift`, `AgentServer.swift` are **frozen at current
size**: anything adding more than ~50 lines goes in an extension file
(`EditorViewController+<Feature>.swift`, `TimelineView+<Feature>.swift`,
`AgentServer+<Feature>.swift`) or a new `…SheetController`, and the frozen
file keeps only the wiring — a stored property, a closure assignment, a
validator arm, a draw call. The pieces extension files build on are therefore
internal, not private. Pitfalls: a selector declared `@objc` on an extension
needs NO forward in the frozen file (a second declaration is an error); a
command whose body sits at the foot of a non-extension feature file carries
its validator arm there too, or the item falls through to the closing
`return true`; `handleEditorCharacter`'s bare-key `switch` matches in SOURCE
order, so a bare `case "x"` goes BELOW any modified `case "x" where …`; and
`handleEditorKey` refuses while a sheet is attached, because a sheet is
window-modal and the preview panel's forwarded keys would otherwise reach
the key map behind it.
